line: Misaeng means "not yet alive": on a go board, a group of stones that is neither alive nor dead.
It started when his uncle brought a set of stones round to the flat. The boy nearly swallowed a few, and loved them anyway.
Go on, then. Where would you play?
beats.speaker: un

line: Baduk is good for concentration, his uncle said, and his mother gladly paid for the neighbourhood class. Soon he was winning his uncle's and his father's bets back from the man who ran the laundromat.

Next came an academy run by a strong amateur. His mother was against it, and nobody expected him to conquer the baduk world, but no one could stop a nine-year-old who got up at dawn to work through his problem book.
Then a professional's dojang, paid for by a sponsor who believed in him. People called him a prodigy, and the word soothed his parents like a sedative.
Then his father's company went under.
At eleven he joined the trainees' room: rows of boards, and children who all meant to turn professional.

args: Trainees have until eighteen to turn professional. He is eighteen now, and this is his last chance.

line: At home, his parents cut out newspaper stories about Lee Chang-ho and Lee Sedol, their rankings and their prize money.
A baduk game is scored in points, and a draw is impossible: the smallest margin is half a point. For seven years he has lost that way, over and over.
He played it perfectly, and he's still half a point short. It's over.
Only now does he see his father's wrinkles, and how dull his mother's eyes have gone.
The day he leaves is an ordinary day. It feels as if he'll be back tomorrow, losing to younger kids again. He hasn't changed; everyone else has, and the colour has drained out of the world.
His friends from the trainees' room turned pro. They ask if he's really quitting, and he has no answer.
It wasn't talent, or luck, or all those half-point losses, or playing between part-time jobs. Those reasons would hurt too much. So he tells himself he just didn't try hard enough.
He walks away dropping stones from his pocket, a few at a time.
Because he didn't try hard enough, he had to come out into the world. Because he didn't try hard enough, he was thrown away.
At home he puts his game records out with the rubbish, along with his board.
Not long after he quit, his father died.
The family opened a small restaurant to get by, and it failed. His mother worked on building sites until her body gave out, and then she could barely get out of bed.
He studied for the high-school equivalency exam between part-time jobs. In the bathroom, he washed her back.
Then he did his military service.

args: He is home from the army: no degree, no trade, and a mother to look after.

line: Your old sponsor was asking after you, the man who paid for all your baduk. Go and see him.
beats.speaker: mo

line: A friend of mine runs a trading company, One International. I've spoken to him. He's the only one there who knows about your baduk, and it'll be a simple interview.
beats.speaker: sp

line: But your résumé is thin, and you'll be going in with nothing. Some people will call you a parachute: someone who only got in through connections.
beats.speaker: sp

line: As the city lights come on, office workers spill out to drink, flatter and head home. He'll start from the bottom like everyone else, and this time he won't fail the way he failed at baduk.
If there's a light I'm meant to keep burning, I'll take responsibility for it. But is there a light allowed for someone like me?
On the morning of his first day, he sleeps through the alarm twice. His mother ties his tie for him.

Across the city that same Wednesday, Oh Sang-sik, a section head at One International, is hiking up a mountain with his three sons. He has forgotten an eleven o'clock meeting with a buyer from overseas. On the summit, his phone rings: it's his own boss, the department head.
Where are you? The buyer's waiting, and if he walks out, we're both finished. I'm sending today's new hire. We're in no position to be picky.
beats.speaker: ms_bujang

line: He makes it to the car, but the road into the city is crawling: five hundred metres in half an hour.
Someone at a workshop said most fear is irrational...
beats.speaker: ms_oh_hike

line: Shall I tell you about dismissal-notice pay?
beats.speaker: ms_bujang

line: I'm at the Mangwon-dong crossroads, doing twelve kilometres an hour, with eight to go. I'll be thirty minutes late. This fear is completely rational.
beats.speaker: ms_oh_hike

line: Jang's first-day message told him to skip the office and go straight to a café in Jongno. The overseas buyer and his manager, Kang, have been waiting there for an hour. Jang can't talk trade, but he can talk about one thing.
A puzzle? All right. I'm Black, and it's my move?
beats.speaker: by

line: Oh bursts in, thirty minutes late, hiking clothes under his jacket.
Your young man kept us busy. The quiz was fun.
beats.speaker: ks

line: In Oh's car there are paper cups everywhere, and Oh argues a claim down the phone with red eyes. Jang once lost to a trainee just like him: sloppy, red-eyed, bored-looking. He'd taken him for careless, and he'd been wrong.
He's obsessive, and responsible: a man who carries everything himself.

I'm Kim Dong-sik, assistant manager on Sales Team 3. HR will brief you properly when we're back. I'm your buddy, and Section Head Oh is your mentor. First job: take this requisition to General Affairs.
beats.speaker: kd

line: Jang Geu-rae, you'll be an intern with Sales Team 3. In two months the interns sit a PT, a presentation test. Pass it, and you stay on.
beats.speaker: hr

line: Two months, then. No degree, no experience, one phone call from a sponsor. If he fails the PT, he's out, and everyone will know he was only ever a parachute.
Eight weeks to the PT. His first real job is filing, and he means to do it better than anyone.
General Affairs hands over a box of supplies, a glue stick among them.
Sort these files into my folders.
beats.speaker: kd

line: He draws a mind map and designs a better filing system. It takes him all afternoon.
Where are my folders? Who do you think you are?
beats.speaker: kd

line: That filing system belongs to the company. This isn't work you do alone; it's work we do together.
beats.speaker: kd

line: At fifteen he filed his game records his own way, in a system only he ever had to read.
Interns' study group tonight. You're coming. Filing? It'll keep. We're going to work out who the dud is.
beats.speaker: gl

line: He has a whole cabinet to re-sort by morning. The glasses intern steers him out of the door anyway.
I should take the requisition to General Affairs first.
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: The other interns are already sizing each other up. Everyone wants a partner who'll make them look good.
The bar is full of interns pitching PT topics. Every time Jang reaches for his bag to leave, the glasses intern refills his glass and pulls him back down.
Sit, sit. You can't leave before we've picked the dud. Well, we all know who it is.
beats.speaker: gl

line: Ahn Young-yi, top of their intake and the only woman there, has been watching. She catches Jang's sleeve and steers him out of the door, away from the noise.
Hey, new kid. Pull yourself together.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: You haven't said a word all night. You won't learn just by listening.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: And you've got filing due tomorrow, but you're sitting here? Make your own stones safe before you attack.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: It's an old baduk proverb that even people who've never played use. He's lived by it his whole life, and he had to hear it from someone else. He runs back to the office.
You kept him here when you knew he had filing due tomorrow. Come on. You're going to go and apologise.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: Sorry. I shouldn't have kept you out.
beats.speaker: gl

line: On Jang's desk are two ways of filing the same papers: Kim's, which the whole team knows, and Jang's new one, which is better but only he understands. Kim wants his own back. One of them, it seems, has to go.
His system makes sense. The trouble is, everyone on staff already knows the old one.
beats.speaker: ms_ahn

line: In baduk, two groups locked together can sometimes both live, if neither side forces the issue. Ahn has found the way.
Keep Mr. Kim's order for the executives' file, but use Jang's cross-index from the planning stage. Then the departments could actually line up.
beats.speaker: ms_ahn

line: She kept her own group alive, and his too. Both live.
That night he dreams of a board: rows of white stones, and one black.
He's up before the alarm and crushed on the train. The world moves faster than he does.
Better plain and on time than perfect and late.
The PT dates are set: the first week of next month, a whole week at the training centre. There's an individual task and a team task, so start thinking about partners.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: Everyone's going to want you. You've got no confidence and no skills, and if you pair with a sure dud, you shine.
beats.speaker: kd

line: Be careful of whoever comes to you first.
beats.speaker: kd

line: The call to the forwarder about the shipping papers, the B/L. The copies. The floor. All at once.
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: Six weeks to the PT, and he still has no partner.
Whoever your partner is, trust them. As the saying goes, the player inside the game can't see his own moves, but everyone watching can.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: A trainee sits at a board, ringed by onlookers. Everyone watching already knows how it ends.
Do your part, and trust the rest.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: One by one the other interns pair off. Nobody asks him.
Have you picked a partner yet? Meet me on the roof tonight.
beats.speaker: han

line: That night, the intern who asked about partners is waiting for him on the roof.
I'm Han Seok-yul. I came back from the Ulsan plant for the PT.
beats.speaker: han

line: Sente is the initiative: the right to lead the game. He's always handed it over. This time he means to keep it.
Han reels it off: mechanical engineering, contest prizes, plant tours, foreign buyers, even a meal with the president. It's like stones slammed down by the handful.
Team up with me. You can build the PT however you like; just email me your progress.
beats.speaker: han

line: Five weeks to the PT. Han said Jang could build it his way.
After years of fighting alone at a board, the office feels kinder and warmer. He emails Han three ideas for the PT.
Han texts back one word: Again!
At lunch, away from Jang, the glasses intern sidles up to Ahn.
Picked your partner yet? Not Jang, surely.
beats.speaker: gl

line: Jang's with Han. And they say Han made a big mistake in front of a buyer at Ulsan.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: A total dud. Who's going to volunteer for the bomb squad?
beats.speaker: gl

line: Who knows? Maybe Jang's a big dud. A nuclear bomb.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: Jang slips into the restroom and calls Han.
You said I could build it my way.
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: I said you'd share it with me. I never said I'd keep my mouth shut.
beats.speaker: ms_han

line: Then what kind of idea do you want?
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: At the Ulsan plant, Han is told he has one last chance and should go back to a desk if he isn't up to it. In Seoul, Jang sits at his screen beside an abandoned board. The world is far colder and more heartless than he thought.
Four weeks to the PT, and his partner keeps sending his work back.
He works all night on three new ideas, forty pages each. In the morning, Oh tears into a team document he made.
The colours don't match and the boxes are all over the place. What were you doing yesterday? Shrink the boxes.
beats.speaker: oh

line: He slips into an empty meeting room and calls Han.
Well? Should I do it again?
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: ...The second one's good. Let's go with that.
beats.speaker: ms_han

line: He says it as if it were his to decide, and Jang's to obey.
Baduk is a war with a plain winner and loser, and he lived in it for over ten years. He may be a beaten soldier, but he was raised to compete, and he doesn't hand over sente.
Then we chose it together. From here on I'll write the PT my way. I'll keep you posted, but I won't be taking instructions.
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: In Korea, age decides who may talk down to whom. Han is older, and has talked down to him from the start. Now Jang drops the polite forms.
And how old are you, anyway?
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: After too many short nights, he finally falls into a deep sleep, slumped in a chair in an empty meeting room.
His partner's Han Seok-yul, and Han's a talker. I bet Jang's doing all the work.
beats.speaker: kd

line: A smooth talker, and a kid who can't tell he's being used. Some team.
beats.speaker: oh

line: He dreams of his heroes, the great players: Cho Nam-chul, Cho Hunhyun, Lee Chang-ho, Lee Sedol. One by one they fade away. Hasn't he let go of baduk yet?
You were crying in your sleep. So your partner's Han? He'll use anyone to make himself shine.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: An ambitious man is like a tornado. But the eye of a tornado is calm. If you can get to his centre, you two could make it work.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: Wait, that's why I came! The seniors want all the interns out tonight. It's evening already; you slept the whole day.
beats.speaker: ahn

line: He's late to the team dinner, so he has to down three penalty drinks. He laughs along with everyone, and still feels like a guest at someone else's table.
Three weeks to the PT. The interns are graded on everything, and one careless moment can sink any of them.
Anything with figures on it goes in the shredder. Not one of our papers should ever turn up outside this team.
beats.speaker: kd

line: He decides to shred the waybill later with the next batch, and leaves it on his desk: Sales Team 3, DH-14.
Can I borrow your glue? Our supply cabinet's locked and nobody will give me the key.
beats.speaker: sh

line: Kim Seok-ho, an intern on another team, glues his report together at Jang's desk, right on top of the waybill, and hurries off.
Jang hums as he feeds the shredder. Down in the lobby, a yellow sheet slides off the security desk onto the floor, and a passing director taps it with his shoe.
Director! Is this about a team dinner?
beats.speaker: oh

line: Without a word, the director kicks the team's paper box over. His aide hands Oh the waybill: they found it on the lobby floor.
Let's all do our jobs properly, shall we?
beats.speaker: dir

line: By the windows, Oh lines the interns up. Whose desk did that waybill come from?
It was mine. I left it on my desk.
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: Every intern turns to look at him. Three weeks before the PT, it goes on his record.
Kim Seok-ho stares at the floor.
Back at his desk, Oh turns the waybill over. Glued to the back is a torn scrap of someone's weekly report, with a name on it: Kim Seok-ho.
Someone else's scrap, glued to Jang's waybill. Oh means to find out how it got there.
Applause from across the floor. Go, a section head on Sales Team 1, comes over pumping his fists.
My baby intern, Kim Seok-ho! He pulls all-nighters with us, he's newly married, he's the eldest son of an eldest son, and we've just landed the deal.
beats.speaker: go

line: He comes over to our team a lot, to borrow supplies.
beats.speaker: ms_oh

line: Ha! That's my fault. The supply cabinet key's on my key ring.
beats.speaker: go

line: Oh looks at the waybill in his hands: a locked cabinet, a borrowed glue stick, and a scrap with a name on it.
That evening Oh takes Jang and Kim out for a drink, and it isn't even nine before he's tipsy.
Geu-rae didn't do anything wrong today. Being misunderstood is a terrible thing.
beats.speaker: ms_oh

line: At the next table, Sales Team 1 is celebrating its deal, Go and his intern Kim Seok-ho among them.
Jealous, Oh? You snub my intern over a few supplies, and now you want to spoil our win?
beats.speaker: go

line: Get your intern his own glue! Our kid took the blame because yours got glue on a document and dropped it!
beats.speaker: ms_oh

line: It doesn't sink in for Go, but it does for Kim Seok-ho.
Our kid. He called him our kid.
Stay on your toes, punk. The PT's coming.
beats.speaker: ms_oh

line: Late that night, Kim Seok-ho gets home to his one-room flat. The baby is still awake and knows him at once. Her tiny hand closes round his finger.
Not yet. The scrap, the glue, the key... I need to put it together first.
beats.speaker: ms_oh

line: Two weeks to the PT. Every day is a lesson in what the job really is.

At first light he's at Incheon harbour, where cargo meant for Gunsan was unloaded by mistake, some of it damaged. He came to see it for himself; paperwork alone drifts away from what's really happening on site.

Back on the thirteenth floor, Steve Han, head of the Americas textile team, has come to pick a fight with Department Head Kim Bu-ryeon, who runs Sales Teams 1 to 3. They're the same rank, and everyone is watching.
I don't have time for a report this thick. A fat report is just a way for nobody to take responsibility.
beats.speaker: st

line: My team was up all night on it.
beats.speaker: br

line: I need to understand the client, not your catalogue. Who's it for? What's their climate? What do they like? Just tell me what I need.
beats.speaker: st

line: Everyone is playing their own game of baduk. Whoever prepared better ends up happier with the result, and whoever rushed just to keep up has no excuse.
Why would Steve come down on our department head? Out with it.
beats.speaker: oh

line: Steve suggested dinner with the buyers, and I picked the place. I'd had a few drinks.
beats.speaker: go

line: Go had taken a buyer, and Steve, to a dog-meat restaurant and never apologised. Ever since, Steve has been sitting on Sales Team 1's approvals.
And our department head is too sore to apologise. In a way, it's checkmate.
beats.speaker: oh

line: Checkmate: a janggi word, from Korean chess, used by a man who doesn't play baduk. Jang can't help grinning.
You're laughing while your seniors talk?
beats.speaker: kd

line: Apologising is the only way. In baduk, you don't leave dead stones lying on the board. Leave one there, and it grows into a bigger problem.
beats.speaker: ms_jang

line: Then let's play politics with some class. Knowing when to bow your head: that's class. Let's go.
beats.speaker: oh

line: They go looking for Kim Bu-ryeon, only to find him already on the textile floor with Go, apologising to Steve. Then Go asks whether the approvals will go faster now, and everyone laughs.
Jang smiles to himself. The obvious move had been obvious to Department Head Kim too.
Often the obvious move is the hardest one to play. Some things you have to do however hard they are, and some you mustn't do however easy.
That night his mother asks how work was. Fine, he says, and for once it's true.

Two weeks to the PT. There will be dead stones in his own work too, and he'll have to give them up. He still isn't alive on this board, but for the first time he can see how a group like his might live.
